claim: Mice are the most commonly used model animals for itch research and for development of anti-itch drugs.
source: Mice are the most commonly used model animals for itch research and for development of anti-itch drugs.
evidence: This is a statement of established practice in the field, representing common scientific knowledge about animal models in itch research.

claim: Most laboratories manually quantify mouse scratching behavior to assess itch intensity.
source: Most laboratories manually quantify mouse scratching behavior to assess itch intensity.
evidence: This describes current standard practice in the field, representing established knowledge about methodology.

claim: Manual quantification of mouse scratching behavior is labor-intensive and limits large-scale genetic or drug screenings.
source: This process is labor-intensive and limits large-scale genetic or drug screenings.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of manual methods based on their time-consuming nature.

claim: The Scratch-AID system can automatically identify and quantify mouse scratching behavior with high accuracy.
source: In this study, we developed a new system, Scratch-AID (Automatic Itch Detection), which could automatically identify and quantify mouse scratching behavior with high accuracy.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Scratch-AID system includes a custom-designed videotaping box to ensure high-quality and replicable mouse behavior recording.
source: Our system included a custom-designed videotaping box to ensure high-quality and replicable mouse behavior recording and a convolutional recurrent neural network trained with frame-labeled mouse scratching behavior videos, induced by nape injection of chloroquine.
evidence: This describes the design and components of the system developed in the study.

claim: The Scratch-AID system uses a convolutional recurrent neural network trained with frame-labeled mouse scratching behavior videos induced by nape injection of chloroquine.
source: Our system included a custom-designed videotaping box to ensure high-quality and replicable mouse behavior recording and a convolutional recurrent neural network trained with frame-labeled mouse scratching behavior videos, induced by nape injection of chloroquine.
evidence: This describes the neural network architecture and training data used in the study.

claim: The best trained network achieved 97.6% recall and 96.9% precision on previously unseen test videos.
source: The best trained network achieved 97.6% recall and 96.9% precision on previously unseen test videos.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing the trained model on test videos.

claim: Scratch-AID can reliably identify scratching behavior in the acute cheek model.
source: Remarkably, Scratch-AID could reliably identify scratching behavior in other major mouse itch models, including the acute cheek model, the histaminergic model, and a chronic itch model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the system's performance on different itch models.

claim: Scratch-AID can reliably identify scratching behavior in the histaminergic model.
source: Remarkably, Scratch-AID could reliably identify scratching behavior in other major mouse itch models, including the acute cheek model, the histaminergic model, and a chronic itch model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the system's performance on different itch models.

claim: Scratch-AID can reliably identify scratching behavior in a chronic itch model.
source: Remarkably, Scratch-AID could reliably identify scratching behavior in other major mouse itch models, including the acute cheek model, the histaminergic model, and a chronic itch model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the system's performance on different itch models.

claim: Scratch-AID detected significant differences in scratching behavior between control and mice treated with an anti-itch drug.
source: Moreover, our system detected significant differences in scratching behavior between control and mice treated with an anti-itch drug.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the drug screening experiment.

claim: Chronic itch affects about 13–17% of the population.
source: Chronic itch affects about 13–17% of the population (Matterne et al., 2009; Weisshaar and Dalgard, 2009), severely worsening the quality of life of affected patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Chronic itch severely worsens the quality of life of affected patients.
source: Chronic itch affects about 13–17% of the population (Matterne et al., 2009; Weisshaar and Dalgard, 2009), severely worsening the quality of life of affected patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Treatment options for many chronic itch conditions are still limited.
source: Unfortunately, treatment options for many chronic itch conditions are still limited (Yosipovitch et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Mice are the most widely used model animals for studying itch mechanisms and for developing new preclinical anti-itch drugs.
source: Mice are the most widely used model animals for studying itch mechanisms and for developing new preclinical anti-itch drugs (Han et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2009; Solinski et al., 2019; Sun and Chen, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Itch is an unpleasant sensation that provokes the desire to scratch.
source: Since itch is an unpleasant sensation that provokes the desire to scratch (Ikoma et al., 2006), scratching behavior has been assessed as a proxy for itch intensity in mice (Liu et al., 2009; Morita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about the nature of itch.

claim: Scratching behavior has been assessed as a proxy for itch intensity in mice.
source: Since itch is an unpleasant sensation that provokes the desire to scratch (Ikoma et al., 2006), scratching behavior has been assessed as a proxy for itch intensity in mice (Liu et al., 2009; Morita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies and represents established methodology.

claim: Quantification of mouse scratching behavior has been mainly conducted by watching videos and manually counting scratching bouts or the total scratching time.
source: Till now, this quantification process has been mainly conducted by watching videos and manually counting scratching bouts or the total scratching time, which is tedious and time consuming, unavoidably introduces human errors and bias, and limits the large-scale genetic or drug screenings.
evidence: This describes current standard practice in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: Manual quantification of scratching behavior is tedious and time consuming.
source: Till now, this quantification process has been mainly conducted by watching videos and manually counting scratching bouts or the total scratching time, which is tedious and time consuming, unavoidably introduces human errors and bias, and limits the large-scale genetic or drug screenings.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of manual methods.

claim: Manual quantification of scratching behavior unavoidably introduces human errors and bias.
source: Till now, this quantification process has been mainly conducted by watching videos and manually counting scratching bouts or the total scratching time, which is tedious and time consuming, unavoidably introduces human errors and bias, and limits the large-scale genetic or drug screenings.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of manual methods.

claim: Several research groups have tried different strategies to automate the quantification of mouse scratching behavior, including an acoustic recording method.
source: Given the biological importance and the obvious need, several research groups have tried different strategies to automate this process, including an acoustic recording method (Elliott et al., 2017), a method using magnetic field and metal ring to detect paw movement (Mu et al., 2017), and several video analysis-based approaches (Bohnslav et al., 2021; Kobayashi et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019; Sakamoto et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: A method using magnetic field and metal ring to detect paw movement has been developed to automate quantification of mouse scratching behavior.
source: Given the biological importance and the obvious need, several research groups have tried different strategies to automate this process, including an acoustic recording method (Elliott et al., 2017), a method using magnetic field and metal ring to detect paw movement (Mu et al., 2017), and several video analysis-based approaches (Bohnslav et al., 2021; Kobayashi et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019; Sakamoto et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Several video analysis-based approaches have been developed to automate quantification of mouse scratching behavior.
source: Given the biological importance and the obvious need, several research groups have tried different strategies to automate this process, including an acoustic recording method (Elliott et al., 2017), a method using magnetic field and metal ring to detect paw movement (Mu et al., 2017), and several video analysis-based approaches (Bohnslav et al., 2021; Kobayashi et al., 2021; Park et al., 2019; Sakamoto et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Previous automated methods for quantifying mouse scratching behavior have not been widely adopted by other research laboratories.
source: Nevertheless, these methods have not been widely adopted by other research laboratories, due to the uncertain performance of the trained models in different lab environments, the requirement of specialized equipment, and/or inadequate evaluation of these methods in different mouse itch models.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of widespread use of these methods in the field.

claim: Previous automated methods have uncertain performance in different lab environments.
source: Nevertheless, these methods have not been widely adopted by other research laboratories, due to the uncertain performance of the trained models in different lab environments, the requirement of specialized equipment, and/or inadequate evaluation of these methods in different mouse itch models.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of previous methods.

claim: Some previous automated methods require specialized equipment.
source: Nevertheless, these methods have not been widely adopted by other research laboratories, due to the uncertain performance of the trained models in different lab environments, the requirement of specialized equipment, and/or inadequate evaluation of these methods in different mouse itch models.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of previous methods.

claim: Previous automated methods have inadequate evaluation in different mouse itch models.
source: Nevertheless, these methods have not been widely adopted by other research laboratories, due to the uncertain performance of the trained models in different lab environments, the requirement of specialized equipment, and/or inadequate evaluation of these methods in different mouse itch models.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of previous methods.

claim: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are widely used in computer visual recognition tasks.
source: For example, convolutional neural networks (CNN) are widely used in computer visual recognition tasks (Gu et al., 2018), whereas recurrent neural networks (RNN) (Graves, 2013) are developed for analyzing temporal dynamic features.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge in the field of deep learning.

claim: Recurrent neural networks (RNN) are developed for analyzing temporal dynamic features.
source: For example, convolutional neural networks (CNN) are widely used in computer visual recognition tasks (Gu et al., 2018), whereas recurrent neural networks (RNN) (Graves, 2013) are developed for analyzing temporal dynamic features.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge in the field of deep learning.

claim: DeepLabCut can track different body parts in freely moving animals for behavior analysis.
source: For example, DeepLabCut can track different body parts in freely moving animals for behavior analysis (Mathis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: DeepEthogram recognizes and annotates different behaviors of mice and flies.
source: DeepEthogram recognizes and annotates different behaviors of mice and flies (Bohnslav et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The videotaping box consists of two boxes with white acrylic walls joined by a transparent acrylic floor.
source: It consisted of two boxes with white acrylic walls joined by a transparent acrylic floor (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the design of the videotaping box, supported by the figure showing the box.

claim: The top box of the videotaping system has dimensions of Length × Width × Height = 14.68 × 14.68 × 5 cm.
source: The top ('mouse') box (Length × Width × Height = 14.68 × 14.68 × 5 cm) had a lid for mouse access.
evidence: This provides specific measurements of the videotaping box design.

claim: The bottom box of the videotaping system has dimensions of Length × Width × Height = 14.68 × 14.68 × 23.6 cm.
source: The bottom ('camera') box (Length × Width × Height = 14.68 × 14.68 × 23.6 cm) had a door for access to the camera (Logitech C920e Business Webcam).
evidence: This provides specific measurements of the videotaping box design.

claim: The camera recorded mouse behavior from the bottom at 30 frames per second.
source: A mouse could freely move inside the top box, and a camera recorded mouse behavior from the bottom (30 frames/s).
evidence: This describes the recording parameters used in the study.

claim: The bottom view can clearly capture the key body parts involved in scratching behavior, such as the scratching hind paw and mouth, and their movements in great details.
source: Compared to the top or side views, the bottom view can clearly capture the key body parts involved in scratching behavior, such as the scratching hind paw and mouth, and their movements in great details (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the video showing the bottom view recording.

claim: Forty scratching videos from 10 adult wildtype C57 mice (5 males and 5 females, 2- to 3-month-old) were recorded.
source: Forty scratching videos from 10 adult wildtype C57 mice (5 males and 5 females, 2- to 3-month-old) were recorded (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the dataset used for training and testing the model.

claim: A scratching train usually contains four phases: start, scratching bout, paw licking, and end.
source: Each episode of scratching, here defined as a scratching train, usually contained four phases: start (lifting the scratching hind paw toward the affected skin), scratching bout (rhythmic movement of hind paw against the affected skin), paw licking (putting the scratching hind paw into the mouth and licking), and end (putting down the scratching hind paw back to the floor) (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This describes the observed behavior patterns, supported by figure and video.

claim: The cycle of scratching bout and paw licking might occur once or repeat multiple times, depending on the itch intensity and the internal state of the mouse.
source: The cycle of scratching bout and paw licking might occur once or repeat multiple times, depending on the itch intensity and the internal state of the mouse.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of scratching behavior.

claim: The total scratching time is the sum of durations of all scratching trains.
source: The total scratching time is the sum of durations of all scratching trains, which is an effective parameter to quantify the scratching behavior and assess itch intensity.
evidence: This defines a measurement parameter used in the study.

claim: The total scratching time is an effective parameter to quantify the scratching behavior and assess itch intensity.
source: The total scratching time is the sum of durations of all scratching trains, which is an effective parameter to quantify the scratching behavior and assess itch intensity.
evidence: This is supported by established practice in the field.

claim: Manual annotation results were produced by 10 human observers.
source: Our manual annotation results were produced by 10 human observers, thus reflecting an averaged precision of the manual quantification process.
evidence: This describes the methodology for creating the manual annotation dataset.

claim: The scratching hind paw displays rhythmic movement during scratching behavior.
source: One of the most obvious dynamic features was the rhythmic movement of the scratching hind paw (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The CRNN contains a CNN (ResNet-18) that extracts static features.
source: The CRNN contained a CNN (ResNet-18 He et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) that extracts static features, such as the relative position of different body parts, an RNN (two-layer bidirectional gated recurrent unit [GRU]; Dey and Salem, 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) that extracts dynamic features, such as the rhythmic movement of the scratching hind paw in consecutive frames, and a fully connected layer (the classifier) to combine the features extracted by both CNN and RNN and generate the prediction output.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the neural network designed for the study.

claim: The CRNN contains an RNN (two-layer bidirectional GRU) that extracts dynamic features.
source: The CRNN contained a CNN (ResNet-18 He et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) that extracts static features, such as the relative position of different body parts, an RNN (two-layer bidirectional gated recurrent unit [GRU]; Dey and Salem, 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) that extracts dynamic features, such as the rhythmic movement of the scratching hind paw in consecutive frames, and a fully connected layer (the classifier) to combine the features extracted by both CNN and RNN and generate the prediction output.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the neural network designed for the study.

claim: The CRNN contains a fully connected layer (the classifier) to combine the features extracted by both CNN and RNN and generate the prediction output.
source: The CRNN contained a CNN (ResNet-18 He et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) that extracts static features, such as the relative position of different body parts, an RNN (two-layer bidirectional gated recurrent unit [GRU]; Dey and Salem, 2017; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) that extracts dynamic features, such as the rhythmic movement of the scratching hind paw in consecutive frames, and a fully connected layer (the classifier) to combine the features extracted by both CNN and RNN and generate the prediction output.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the neural network designed for the study.

claim: The 40 videos were randomly split into 80% for training dataset (32 videos from 8 mice) and 20% for test dataset (8 videos from 2 mice).
source: The 40 videos were randomly split into two parts, 80% of them (32 videos from 8 mice) were assigned to the training dataset and 20% of them (8 videos from 2 mice) to the test dataset (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the methodology for splitting the dataset.

claim: The average duration of one cycle of scratching bout and paw licking was around 30 frames in the CQ triggered acute nape itch model.
source: In CQ triggered acute nape itch model, the average duration of one cycle of scratching bout and paw licking was around 30 frames (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: A range of input length from 3 to 45 frames was tested for model training.
source: Thus, we tested a range of input length from 3 to 45 frames for model training.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for optimizing the model.

claim: After 10 epochs, the prediction accuracy reached a plateau.
source: After 10 epochs (one epoch means the training covers the complete training dataset for one round), the accuracy reached a plateau (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The prediction accuracies were more than 0.98 for all input lengths.
source: The prediction accuracies were more than 0.98 for all input length, improving slightly with the increase of the input length (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Prediction accuracy improved slightly with the increase of the input length.
source: The prediction accuracies were more than 0.98 for all input length, improving slightly with the increase of the input length (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For all different combinations of training and test videos, F1 scores were all above 0.9.
source: To rule out the possibility that the good performance of our models was due to a specific combination of the training and test datasets, we rotated the training and test videos for cross-validation. For all different combination of training and test videos, F1 scores were all above 0.9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), supporting the stable and high performance of our prediction models.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The prediction model performed better with increased input length.
source: In addition, the prediction model performed better with the increased input length (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The best model was the one trained with videos 1–32 with the input length of 45 (N = 45).
source: The best model, the one trained with videos 1–32 with the input length of 45 (N = 45), was selected for additional analyses and tests.
evidence: This describes the selection of the best performing model based on the experimental results.

claim: The average recall and precision of manual annotation were 95.1% and 94.2%, respectively.
source: This performance was similar to or even slightly better than that of manual annotation, which had an average recall and precision of 95.1% and 94.2%, respectively (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The average discrepancy of the model prediction compared to reference annotation was 1.9%.
source: When comparing the total scratching time to the reference annotation, the average discrepancy of the model prediction was 1.9% whereas that of manual annotation was 2.1% (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The average discrepancy of manual annotation compared to reference annotation was 2.1%.
source: When comparing the total scratching time to the reference annotation, the average discrepancy of the model prediction was 1.9% whereas that of manual annotation was 2.1% (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The correlation between the model prediction and the reference annotation was 0.98.
source: The correlation between the model prediction and the reference annotation was 0.98, similar to the manual annotation results (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The trained neural network model focused on the scratching hind paw to recognize mouse scratching behavior.
source: The most salient parts were centered around the scratching hind paw in the scratching frames (Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the prediction model focused on the features of the scratching hind paw.
evidence: This is supported by saliency map analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The dominant prediction error of the trained neural network model was Type 3 error (blurred boundary), accounting for around 3% of the total scratching frames.
source: We found that the dominant prediction error of the trained neural network model was Type 3 error, accounting for around 3% of the total scratching frames, followed by Type 2 and 5 errors accounting for around 1% (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: For manual quantification, the major errors came from Types 3 and 4, accounting for 10% and 8% of the total scratching frames, respectively.
source: For manual quantification, the major errors came from Types 3 and 4, accounting for 10% and 8% of the total scratching frames, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: All false positive scratching trains predicted by the model were shorter than 10 frames (0.3 s).
source: For Type 1 error of the model prediction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C1–C3), the durations of all false positive scratching trains were shorter than 10 frames (0.3 s) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C2) and temporarily close to a real scratching train (within 30 frames, <1 s) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C3).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: All missed scratching trains (Type 2 error) were shorter than 40 frames (<1.3 s).
source: The models might miss short scratching trains, hence caused the Type 2 error. Indeed, all missed scratching trains were shorter than 40 frames (<1.3 s) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D1, D2).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: For all scratching trains lasting less than 30 frames (<1 s), 18.5% of them were missed by the model prediction.
source: For all scratching trains lasting less than 30 frames (<1 s), 18.5% of them were missed by the model prediction.
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data.

claim: The average start and end frame shift of the model prediction were 2.2 and 7.0 frames.
source: The average start and end frame shift of the model prediction were 2.2 and 7.0 frames (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E3), while those of the manual annotation were 11.5 and 12.8 frames (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D1, D2).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The average start and end frame shift of manual annotation were 11.5 and 12.8 frames.
source: The average start and end frame shift of the model prediction were 2.2 and 7.0 frames (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E3), while those of the manual annotation were 11.5 and 12.8 frames (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D1, D2).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The start of a scratching train was more accurately recognized by the model than the end of a scratching train.
source: In addition, the start of a scratching train was more accurately recognized by the model than the end of a scratching train (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E3).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: All missed intervals (Type 4 error) were shorter than 30 frames (<1 s).
source: Type 4 error was caused when two adjacent scratching trains were too close to each other and were predicted as one scratching train (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F1–F3). All missed intervals were shorter than 30 frames (<1 s) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F2).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: More than 80% of mispredicted intervals in Type 5 error were within or partially overlapped with a paw licking phase.
source: When reviewing these intervals, we found that more than 80% of them were within or partially overlapped with a paw licking phase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G3), especially when the duration of the paw licking was more than 30 frames (Figure 3—figure supplement 5F).
evidence: This is supported by error analysis data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The Scratch-AID prediction had 93.4% recall, 94.8% precision, and 0.941 F1 score for the cheek model.
source: The Scratch-AID prediction had 93.4% recall, 94.8% precision, and 0.941 F1 score (Figure 5B), while those of manual quantification were 96.0%, 88.6%, and 0.919 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Manual quantification had 96.0% recall, 88.6% precision, and 0.919 F1 score for the cheek model.
source: The Scratch-AID prediction had 93.4% recall, 94.8% precision, and 0.941 F1 score (Figure 5B), while those of manual quantification were 96.0%, 88.6%, and 0.919 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The correlation between the Scratch-AID prediction and reference annotation was 0.9926 for the cheek model.
source: The correlation between the Scratch-AID prediction and reference annotation was 0.9926, and that of the manual quantification was 0.9876 (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The correlation between manual quantification and reference annotation was 0.9876 for the cheek model.
source: The correlation between the Scratch-AID prediction and reference annotation was 0.9926, and that of the manual quantification was 0.9876 (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The recall, precision, and F1 score from the Scratch-AID prediction for the histamine model were 96.6%, 90.91%, and 0.936.
source: The recall, precision, and F1 score from the Scratch-AID prediction were 96.6%, 90.91%, and 0.936 (Figure 5H), while those of the manual annotation were 96.3%, 80.5%, and 0.877 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The recall, precision, and F1 score from manual annotation for the histamine model were 96.3%, 80.5%, and 0.877.
source: The recall, precision, and F1 score from the Scratch-AID prediction were 96.6%, 90.91%, and 0.936 (Figure 5H), while those of the manual annotation were 96.3%, 80.5%, and 0.877 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The correlation between the Scratch-AID prediction and reference annotation is 0.9707 for the histamine model.
source: The correlation between the Scratch-AID prediction and reference annotation is 0.9707, and that of the manual quantification is 0.9895 (Figure 5J, K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The correlation between manual quantification and reference annotation is 0.9895 for the histamine model.
source: The correlation between the Scratch-AID prediction and reference annotation is 0.9707, and that of the manual quantification is 0.9895 (Figure 5J, K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Dynamic features of spontaneous scratching behavior under chronic itch conditions were different from those exhibited by the CQ acute itch model.
source: Noticeably, dynamic features of spontaneous scratching behavior under this chronic itch condition were different from those exhibited by the CQ acute itch model: the total scratching time was less for the same given period of time (20 min) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and the average duration of the scratching trains was shorter (53 frames on average) than the acute scratching behavior induced by CQ (280 frames on average) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The recall, precision, and F1 score of the Scratch-AID prediction for the chronic itch model were 84.1%, 88.5%, and 0.862, respectively.
source: Despite these considerable differences, the recall, precision, and F1 score of the Scratch-AID prediction were 84.1%, 88.5%, and 0.862, respectively, compared to 84.1%, 66.3%, and 0.740 of manual annotation (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The recall, precision, and F1 score of manual annotation for the chronic itch model were 84.1%, 66.3%, and 0.740.
source: Despite these considerable differences, the recall, precision, and F1 score of the Scratch-AID prediction were 84.1%, 88.5%, and 0.862, respectively, compared to 84.1%, 66.3%, and 0.740 of manual annotation (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The correlation between the model prediction and reference annotation was 0.9845 for the chronic itch model.
source: The correlation between the model prediction and reference annotation was 0.9845 (Figure 6D), which was comparable to the manual annotation 0.9887 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The correlation between manual annotation and reference annotation was 0.9887 for the chronic itch model.
source: The correlation between the model prediction and reference annotation was 0.9845 (Figure 6D), which was comparable to the manual annotation 0.9887 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Quantification of the total scratching time using the Scratch-AID showed a significant reduction with Benadryl treatment.
source: Quantification of the total scratching time (frames) using the Scratch-AID showed a significant reduction with Benardryl treatment (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Manual annotation showed similar results to Scratch-AID in detecting the effect of Benadryl treatment.
source: Similar results were found by manual annotation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Variable video recording condition is a major barrier that has prevented the adoption of a trained neural network by different laboratories.
source: Variable video recording condition is a major barrier that has prevented the adoption of a trained neural network by different laboratories.
evidence: This is an inference about the challenges in the field based on the authors' understanding.

source: The trained models usually do not perform well with videos recorded under different conditions (illumination, field size, image resolution, magnification of mice, image angle, backgrounds, etc.).
evidence: This is an inference based on known limitations of machine learning models.

claim: The performance of a prediction model positively correlates with the size of the training dataset.
source: In general, the performance of a prediction model positively corelates with the size of the training dataset.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: ResNet and GRU make a good combination of deep learning architecture for analyzing animal behaviors.
source: Our study shows that ResNet and GRU make a good combination of deep learning architecture for analyzing animal behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of the study.

claim: The accuracy plateau was achieved after only 10 epochs of training.
source: In addition, our network design is highly efficient that the accuracy plateau was achieved after only 10 epochs of training.
evidence: This is supported by the training data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Scratch-AID is the first deep learning-based system that can achieve high accuracy and broad generalization for quantifying mouse scratching behavior.
source: As far as we are aware, this is the first deep learning-based system that can achieve such high accuracy and broad generalization.

claim: A model trained with CQ induced acute nape itch videos could reliably recognize scratching behavior in other itch models.
source: It is remarkable that a model trained with CQ induced acute nape itch videos could reliably recognize scratching behavior in other itch models, even when the body sites (nape vs. cheek) or the dynamics of scratching behavior (e.g., acute vs. chronic itch, different pruritogens) were different.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing performance on different itch models.

claim: The Scratch-AID system is ready to replace manual quantification.
source: Combined with the well-trained prediction model that has a comparable performance as manual quantification, the Scratch-AID system is ready to replace the manual quantification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the performance data of the system.
